title: The ten days
hook: the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are for making amends

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three books, and the middle one still open. Your line was write us in. Did you do one thing that belongs in your line? Today, the days when the middle book is still being written. Day six hundred fifty.

There's a particular feeling to the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The holiday food is in the fridge. Work and school have started again. Life looks ordinary. But people who keep these days describe a hum underneath, like the week before a big exam, or the days before a long-delayed conversation. Small changes show up, too. Words in the daily prayers shift. Someone you haven't heard from in a year calls, a bit awkwardly, to say they're sorry.
screen: `LIFE LOOKS ORDINARY.` → `A HUM UNDERNEATH.` → `AN AWKWARD PHONE CALL.`

segments.voice: These are the aseret yemei teshuvah, the ten days of return, counting Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 18a, reads a verse from Isaiah as being about these days: "Seek ye the LORD while He may be found, call ye upon Him while He is near." While He is near. These are the near days. The daily Amidah changes to match. All year, one blessing ends: the holy God. For these ten days it ends: the holy King. Forget, and in many traditions you go back and say it again. Avinu Malkeinu, our father, our king, is said at many services. Some people take on stricter habits for just these days. And the center of it all is teshuvah, usually translated repentance, though the word means return, turning back. Maimonides lays out what it involves. You recognize what you did wrong. You regret it. You say it out loud, in words, to God. And you resolve not to do it again. And then he gives a test for whether teshuvah is complete. You find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation, the same person, the same chance, and this time you choose differently. Not because you can't. Because you've changed. That's the work of these days. Not grand gestures. Specific turns, one person, one habit, one sentence. The ten days are short on purpose. Long enough to do something. Short enough that you can't put it off.
screen: `TEN DAYS OF RETURN.` · `SEEK WHILE HE IS NEAR.` · `THE HOLY GOD BECOMES THE HOLY KING.` · `SAME SITUATION, NEW CHOICE.` · then, large: `TEN DAYS TO TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: apologize to one person. Sit, and let a face come to mind: someone you hurt this year, in a big way or a small one. Walk through Maimonides' steps quietly. What did I do? Do I regret it? Can I say it in words? What would I do differently? Then draft the first sentence of an apology, the actual words you'd say or text. Keep it simple and specific. If you pray, you can also bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Aseret yemei teshuvah. The ten days of return, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, when the prayers say the holy King.
Your line: ten days to turn. Today, send the apology you drafted, or set a time to say it. Day six hundred fifty.

howItsDone: During the Ten Days of Repentance, Jews change wording in the Amidah (HaMelech HaKadosh), say Avinu Malkeinu, add selichot, and many seek out people they have wronged to apologize before Yom Kippur.

what it means: a short, near window to make specific turns, one person and one habit at a time.
what a scholar hears: Rosh Hashanah 18a on Isaiah 55:6, and Maimonides' Hilchot Teshuvah 2:1–2 on complete return.

sources.quoted: Seek ye the LORD while He may be found, call ye upon Him while He is near

notes: Rosh Hashanah 18a links Isaiah 55:6 to the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur; confirm.
HaMelech HaKadosh: forgetting it requires repeating the Amidah per Shulchan Arukh OC 582:1; 'in many traditions' used.
Maimonides' steps (recognize, regret, confess verbally, resolve) and the test of complete teshuvah: Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1, 2:1–2; confirm.
Day 652 covers asking forgiveness before Yom Kippur (Mishnah Yoma 8:9); this day keeps to the ten days and Maimonides' steps.
